title: Why is `WHERE col LIKE '%term%'` slow (leading wildcard forces a full scan), and how does full-text search fix it (a `tsvector` column + GIN inverted index, with stemming and ranking) — and when do you reach for Elasticsearch instead?
shortTitle: Why LIKE '%term%' is slow, full-text search, and when to reach for Elasticsearch
topicTitle: SQL Basics — SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY

s1_definition.profdef: `LIKE '%term%'` is slow because a leading wildcard means the match can start anywhere in the string, so a B-tree index (which is ordered by prefix) cannot be used and the database must scan every row. Full-text search fixes this by precomputing a `tsvector` of normalized, stemmed tokens and building a GIN inverted index that maps each token to the rows containing it, turning substring scanning into an index lookup with stemming and relevance ranking. Elasticsearch is the choice when you need distributed full-text search at scale with rich relevance, faceting, fuzzy matching, and analytics beyond what a relational full-text extension offers.
s1_definition.analogy: Searching the National Bank's transaction descriptions with `LIKE '%rent%'` is like asking a clerk to read every line of every page because "rent" could appear anywhere in a sentence. Full-text search instead builds an index at the back of the book listing every meaningful word and the exact pages it appears on, so the clerk jumps straight to the pages mentioning "rent." Elasticsearch is a dedicated search building for when one book is not enough and you have millions of documents spread across many shelves.
s1_definition.oneliner: A leading wildcard forces a full scan; a tsvector plus GIN inverted index turns word search into an index lookup, and Elasticsearch is for distributed, rich, large-scale search.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `LIKE '%term%'` is slow because a leading wildcard means the match can start anywhere in the string, so a B-tree index (which is ordered by prefix) cannot be used and the database must scan every row. Full-text search fixes this by precomputing a `tsvector` of normalized, stemmed tokens and building a GIN inverted index that maps each token to the rows containing it, turning substring scanning into an index lookup with stemming and relevance ranking. Elasticsearch is the choice when you need distributed full-text search at scale with rich relevance, faceting, fuzzy matching, and analytics beyond what a relational full-text extension offers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Searching the National Bank's transaction descriptions with `LIKE '%rent%'` is like asking a clerk to read every line of every page because "rent" could appear anywhere in a sentence. Full-text search instead builds an index at the back of the book listing every meaningful word and the exact pages it appears on, so the clerk jumps straight to the pages mentioning "rent." Elasticsearch is a dedicated search building for when one book is not enough and you have millions of documents spread across many shelves.

**One line to remember:** A leading wildcard forces a full scan; a tsvector plus GIN inverted index turns word search into an index lookup, and Elasticsearch is for distributed, rich, large-scale search.

sections.s2_technical:
A B-tree index is ordered alphabetically by the start of the value. That is why `LIKE 'rent%'` — a trailing wildcard — can use an index: the database seeks to entries beginning with "rent." But `LIKE '%rent%'` has a leading wildcard, meaning the match could begin at any position in the string. There is no ordered starting point to seek to, so the database must read every row and test it. On a large table that is a full sequential scan, and it gets slower as the table grows.

Full-text search solves a different, better-shaped problem: matching words, not arbitrary substrings. In PostgreSQL you convert text into a `tsvector`, which is a normalized list of lexemes — words lowercased, stripped of punctuation, and reduced to their stem so that "rented", "renting", and "rent" all become the same lexeme. You store this in a column, for example `to_tsvector('english', description)`, and build a GIN index on it. A GIN index is an inverted index: it maps each lexeme to the list of rows that contain it, exactly like the index at the back of a book.

A search then becomes `WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'rent')`, which looks up the lexeme in the inverted index and returns matching rows directly, without scanning. Because of stemming, a search for "payment" also finds "payments" and "paying," which plain LIKE cannot do. You also get relevance ranking with `ts_rank`, so the most relevant rows come first, and you can search for phrases and boolean combinations.

The practical setup keeps the tsvector in a stored generated column so it updates automatically, and the GIN index on it keeps lookups fast. This handles the vast majority of in-application search needs — searching transaction descriptions, customer notes, product names — without leaving your relational database, keeping search consistent with your transactional data.

You reach for Elasticsearch when you outgrow what the relational full-text feature offers. That means: search across tens of millions of documents that must be distributed and sharded across a cluster; rich relevance scoring with custom analyzers, synonyms, and boosting; typo tolerance through fuzzy matching; faceted navigation and aggregations for search-driven dashboards; autocomplete and suggesters; and very high search query throughput that you want isolated from your transactional database. Elasticsearch is a dedicated, horizontally scalable search engine, but it is a separate system you must keep in sync with your source of truth, usually through change-data-capture, and it is eventually consistent. So the rule is: use PostgreSQL full-text search when the data and scale fit comfortably in your relational database; move to Elasticsearch when scale, relevance richness, or search-specific features justify running and syncing a separate search cluster.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, support staff search transaction descriptions for words like "rent" or "salary" using `LIKE '%rent%'`. As the table grows to millions of rows, every search does a full scan and takes seconds. This is exactly why a leading wildcard is slow — no index can be used.

Problem 2 — A search for "payment" misses rows that say "payments" or "paying." This is exactly what full-text search fixes with stemming — all three reduce to the same lexeme.

Problem 3 — Eventually the bank wants typo-tolerant search ("renr" should still find "rent"), faceting, and search across hundreds of millions of documents at high throughput. This is exactly when you reach for Elasticsearch.

We will build a `TransactionSearchService` using a PostgreSQL `tsvector` column with a GIN index and ranked results, and show the conceptual Elasticsearch path for when the bank outgrows it.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__fulltext.sql
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount       DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    description  TEXT NOT NULL,
    -- stored generated tsvector: normalized, stemmed lexemes kept in sync automatically
    search_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', description)) STORED
);

-- GIN inverted index: maps each lexeme → rows containing it. Turns search into a lookup.
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_fts ON transactions USING GIN (search_vector);

INSERT INTO transactions (account_id, amount, description) VALUES
 ('SAV2001', 25000.00, 'Monthly rent payment to landlord'),
 ('SAV2001', 80000.00, 'Salary credited by employer'),
 ('CUR3001', 12000.00, 'Rental maintenance and paying society dues');

-- SLOW (full scan, leading wildcard, cannot use any index):
-- SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE description LIKE '%rent%';

-- FAST (GIN inverted-index lookup + stemming: finds rent, rental, renting):
-- SELECT txn_id, ts_rank(search_vector, q) AS rank
-- FROM transactions, to_tsquery('english','rent') q
-- WHERE search_vector @@ q ORDER BY rank DESC;
```

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/search-service-1.0.0.jar

# Prove LIKE does a Seq Scan but full-text uses the GIN index
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE description LIKE '%rent%';"
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions, to_tsquery('english','rent') q \
  WHERE search_vector @@ q ORDER BY ts_rank(search_vector,q) DESC;"

# Call the API (stemming: 'rent' also finds 'rental')
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/search?term=rent"

# When you outgrow PostgreSQL FTS, index into Elasticsearch via CDC (Debezium → Kafka → ES)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: support staff search the term "rent" against a transactions table with millions of descriptions.

Step 1: The request reaches `TransactionSearchService`. With the old `LIKE '%rent%'` approach, the database would scan every row because the leading wildcard disables all indexes. That is the slow path we are replacing.

Step 2: With full-text search, the description column already has a stored `search_vector` generated as `to_tsvector('english', description)`. For "Monthly rent payment to landlord," the vector contains stemmed lexemes like `month`, `rent`, `payment`, `landlord`.

Step 3: The service builds a `to_tsquery('english', 'rent')`. PostgreSQL looks up the lexeme `rent` in the GIN inverted index, which directly lists the rows containing it — no scanning.

Step 4: Because of stemming, the same lexeme `rent` also appears for "Rental maintenance," so that row matches too, which plain LIKE for "rent" would also catch but LIKE for "payment" would miss variants.

Step 5: `ts_rank` scores each match by relevance, so the row where "rent" is most prominent ranks first. The service returns ranked results and logs the match count.

Step 6: When the bank later needs typo tolerance, faceting, and hundreds of millions of documents, the same data is streamed via change-data-capture into Elasticsearch, where a dedicated, sharded search cluster serves the queries.

```
2026-10-25 13:51:10 INFO  TransactionSearchService - Full-text search 'rent' matched 2 rows via GIN index
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A query with LIKE and a leading wildcard, like LIKE percent-rent-percent, is slow because a B-tree index is ordered by the start of the value, and a leading wildcard means the match could begin anywhere in the string. There is no ordered starting point to seek to, so the database must read every row and test it — a full sequential scan that only gets worse as the table grows. A trailing wildcard like rent-percent can use an index, but a leading one cannot.

Full-text search fixes this by solving a better-shaped problem: matching words rather than arbitrary substrings. In PostgreSQL I store a tsvector, which is the text normalized into stemmed lexemes so that rented, renting, and rent all collapse to the same token, and I build a GIN index on it. A GIN index is an inverted index that maps each lexeme to the rows containing it, exactly like the index at the back of a book. A search then becomes a match against that index with the double-at operator, which looks up the lexeme and returns matching rows directly without scanning, and I use ts_rank to order results by relevance. Stemming also means a search for payment finds payments and paying, which plain LIKE cannot do. I keep the tsvector as a stored generated column so it stays in sync automatically.

I reach for Elasticsearch when I outgrow what the relational full-text feature offers: search across tens or hundreds of millions of documents that must be sharded across a cluster, rich relevance with custom analyzers and synonyms, typo tolerance through fuzzy matching, faceting and aggregations for search dashboards, autocomplete, and very high search throughput I want isolated from the transactional database. Elasticsearch is a dedicated, horizontally scalable search engine, but it is a separate system I must keep in sync with the source of truth through change-data-capture, and it is eventually consistent.

At the National Bank of India our support team searched transaction descriptions with LIKE and a leading wildcard, and searches took seconds once the table grew to millions of rows while also missing word variants. I added a generated tsvector column with a GIN index and ranked results, so searches became index lookups that returned in milliseconds and matched stemmed variants like rent and rental together. When we later needed typo tolerance and faceting across hundreds of millions of documents, we streamed the data into Elasticsearch through change-data-capture. The rule I always state is that a leading wildcard forces a full scan, a tsvector plus a GIN inverted index turns word search into an index lookup, and Elasticsearch is for distributed, feature-rich, large-scale search.
